narrative:
The model estimated a 63.8% probability that you will fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning that in comparable cases failure is considered more likely than passing. Because law school admission here depends on this predicted risk, your application was denied.

The denial was driven primarily by three factors, in order of influence. Your family income bracket was the strongest factor and it pushed the prediction toward failure; among accepted students, an upper-middle background was more common (45.4%) than a middle background (34.8%), which is the group you reported. Your first-year academic decile was the second-strongest factor and also pushed toward failure: your decile of 5 sits below the accepted-student average of 6. Your LSAT score contributed the smallest push among the top three, also toward failure; at 39 it is above the accepted average of about 37, but it still added modestly to the risk estimate rather than offsetting the other factors.

To improve future applications, consider retaking the LSAT only if practice scores show clear gains, address your early academic record through additional coursework or a strong post-baccalaureate record, and seek admissions advising about programs whose review weighs broader evidence. You may also strengthen your bar-readiness profile before reapplying.
